tips.title: Choosing the Right Cement for ABS vs Polystyrene
tips.text: Tamiya Extra Thin Cement bonds polystyrene perfectly by melting the plastic together, but it struggles with ABS parts found in many modern kits (breeches, gun barrels, ICM and Arma Hobby aircraft propellers). For ABS, switch to Tamiya ABS & Polystyrene Cement in the green bottle, which contains ABS-compatible solvents. Apply sparingly with a fine brush to both surfaces, press together for 10 seconds, and let cure for 24 hours before sanding. Test the bond on a spare sprue first.

tips.title: Selecting the Right Paint Type for Weathering
tips.text: For realistic weathering, use Vallejo Model Air acrylic paints for your base coat and AK Interactive and AMMO by Mig Jimenez acrylic washes and filters. Acrylics are water-based, non-toxic, and offer a wide range of colors. They're also easier to control and clean up than enamels. For lacquers, consider Vallejo Airbrush Thinner for thinning and Citadel Lacquer Thinner for cleanup. Always test paint consistency and flow on a test surface first.

tips.title: Choosing the Right Sandpaper Grits
tips.text: For sanding seams and preparing surfaces, start with 180-220 grit sandpaper for removing mold lines and filling imperfections. Use a light touch and work in one direction to avoid scratches. For finer sanding before painting, switch to 320-400 grit sandpaper. For the smoothest finish, use 600-800 grit sandpaper before applying a primer. Wet sanding with micro-mesh pads can achieve mirror-like finishes.

tips.title: Filling Gaps: Vallejo vs Tamiya Putty
tips.text: Vallejo Plastic Putty is thicker and sticks better to vertical surfaces than Tamiya Putty, making it ideal for filling deep gaps. Apply Vallejo Plastic Putty with a toothpick or brush, let it dry, then scrape off excess with a sharp blade. Tamiya Putty is thinner, great for fine crevices, and easier to sand. For hard-to-reach gaps, mix Tamiya Extra Thin Cement with baking soda to create a custom gap-filling paste. Let it dry, then sand flush.

tips.title: Photo-Etch vs Resin Detail Parts
tips.text: Choose photo-etch (PE) for intricate, thin details (lattice work, railings, etc.) found in Eduard, ICM, and AFV Club sets. PE is stronger and more realistic than plastic but requires careful cutting, bending, and glueing. Resin detail parts from brands like Clear Prop Models and Special H offer high detail and no bending, but they're delicate and harder to clean up. For the best of both worlds, combine PE and resin details in your build.
